tldr: We propose HiTac-WAM, a tactile world action model that forecasts tactile outcomes of candidate actions in a directed hierarchy following physical dependencies (contact state -> 3D deformation field -> slip risk). It uses these forecasts for pre-execution action selection and runtime discrepancy detection with replanning. In real-robot experiments, it significantly boosted task success rate from 31.1% with single-candidate execution to 72.2%.
hero_caption: Overall overview of HiTac-WAM. (a) Candidate actions may look plausible visually but fail physically. (b) HiTac-WAM forecasts tactile states through a hierarchy of contact, deformation, and slip risk to select the best action. (c) The full system substantially improves success rates across three real-robot tasks.
overview:
In dexterous robot manipulation, contact between the fingertips and objects often determines success or failure. However, in world action models (WAMs) that jointly predict future video and actions, contact surfaces are easily occluded. As a result, actions that look plausible visually can actually fail due to insufficient pressure, slippage, or jamming.

To address this, the authors developed HiTac-WAM, which directly forecasts how fingertip touch will evolve before executing an action. Instead of predicting touch as a single image or latent representation, it factorizes tactile forecasting into a physically grounded hierarchy (contact state -> 3D deformation field -> slip risk): contact occurs first, contact causes deformation, and both govern slip. The architecture introduces a directed attention mask that routes context from video and action to touch only, along with stop-gradient conditioning across stages.

The authors evaluated the method on three contact-rich tasks—chip grasping, blackboard erasing, and USB insertion—using a 6-DoF robot arm equipped with dual fingertip tactile sensors. The directed hierarchy reduced 3D displacement error by 17.6% and improved slip detection by 60.4%. Forecast-guided candidate selection increased the success rate from 31.1% to 61.1%, and monitoring predicted vs. observed tactile states for corrective replanning achieved an overall 72.2% success rate.
contributions: Proposed a hierarchical tactile forecasting architecture connecting contact state, 3D deformation, and slip risk with stop-gradients based on physical dependencies.
Designed a directed attention mask that passes video and action context exclusively to tactile queries without degrading video and action generation quality.
Built a ranking mechanism that combines tactile forecast costs and task-progress estimates across candidate action chunks to select the optimal action.
Demonstrated an execution verification and recovery mechanism that retains the selected forecast as a reference to detect physical discrepancies online and trigger safe replanning.

sections.heading: Looks Can Be Deceiving: Why Contact-Rich Manipulation Demands Tactile Forecasting
sections.summary: While world models that jointly predict video and actions are powerful, occlusions at contact interfaces prevent visual predictions from ruling out physically failing actions. HiTac-WAM forecasts future tactile outcomes for unexecuted candidate actions along physical causal dependencies—contact, 3D deformation, and slip risk—using them for action selection and execution monitoring.
sections.details:
In contact-rich manipulation tasks where the robot deeply interacts with the environment, visual predictions alone fall short. For instance, when sampling multiple candidate action chunks from the same initial state with different noise seeds, the predicted future videos all look plausible: the gripper approaches, the eraser moves, and the connector aligns with the port.

Yet in the real physical world, small unobservable factors—such as one-sided contact, insufficient normal force, incipient slip, or lateral jamming—determine success or failure while showing only subtle visual cues. Existing tactile policies primarily rely on reactive feedback after contact. Prior tactile prediction works either forecast raw images or treat physical quantities independently without modeling physical causal dependencies.

HiTac-WAM is designed around three requirements:
- Factorize tactile forecasts into physically meaningful components (contact state, contact-conditional 3D deformation, and slip risk).
- Accurately pair each candidate action with its specific tactile forecast during candidate evaluation.
- Retain the selected forecast as a time-synchronized reference during execution to detect anomalies through discrepancies with reality.

Under matched training budgets, this design reduced 3D displacement error by 17.6%, improved slip AUPRC by 60.4%, and established the foundation for major success rate gains on real hardware.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of World Models and Tactile Prediction: How It Differs
sections.summary: This section reviews prior works in visual world models, tactile policies, and predictive tactile models. HiTac-WAM stands out by explicitly modeling tactile physical dependencies in a directed hierarchy and unifying it for both pre-execution selection and runtime monitoring.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three research areas:

II-A Visual World Models and Action Generation
World models that plan via video prediction or latent dynamics, as well as multimodal action generators like Diffusion Policy, have advanced rapidly. However, vision-centric models struggle to detect the exact timing of contact, pressure distributions, and incipient slip early enough, making appearance scores unreliable for identifying failures. HiTac-WAM augments action proposals from a pretrained world action model with explicit tactile forecasts.

II-B Visuotactile Models and Tactile Forecasting
Tactile policies and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily react to tactile signals collected during execution, without forecasting contact for unexecuted actions. Meanwhile, existing tactile prediction methods either blend contact, deformation, and slip into a single stream or predict them as isolated targets. HiTac-WAM differentiates itself by modeling these quantities as directed physical dependencies.

II-C Action Selection and Execution Monitoring
Prior works have separately explored ranking action candidates with value functions or model predictions, as well as detecting anomalies for recovery. In contrast, HiTac-WAM provides a unified pipeline: it uses hierarchical tactile forecasts to rank action candidates beforehand, and then reuses that very same selected forecast as a runtime reference trajectory to detect discrepancies and replan.

(b) A hierarchical head connecting contact, deformation, and slip sequentially via stop-gradients. (c) The candidate selection pipeline based on tactile costs and runtime residual monitoring using KDE.

sections.heading: Unraveling Touch in Physical Order: HiTac-WAM's Architecture and Algorithm
sections.summary: This section details the proposed model architecture and operational algorithm. A directed attention mask routes video and action features to tactile queries, predictions propagate through contact, deformation, and slip with stop-gradients, and tactile costs guide action selection while KDE-based discrepancy detection triggers replanning.
sections.details:
III-A Directed Multimodal Context
At current timestep $t$, the model takes the robot's history (multi-view RGB, joint states, dual-hand tactile history, language instruction) and $K$ sampled candidate action chunks $\mathbf{A}_t^{(k)}$. Inside the backbone, a directed attention mask is applied: tactile queries can attend to video and action context, but video and action queries cannot attend to tactile tokens. This preserves the strong video and action generation capabilities of the pretrained WAM while producing future tactile forecasts tailored to each candidate action.

III-B Explicit Hierarchical Tactile Forecast
Tactile states are forecasted following physical causal dependencies:
1. Contact state forecast ($\widehat{C}$): First detects contact presence and extracts contact feature $\mathbf{z}^C$.
2. 3D deformation field forecast ($\Delta\widehat{\mathbf{D}}$): Takes features from the contact head with a stop-gradient $\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{z}^C)$ to predict deformation. To avoid predicting non-zero deformation in free space, it is element-wise gated by contact probability $\widehat{C}$.
3. Slip risk forecast ($\widehat{R}^{\mathrm{slip}}$): Takes the detached contact decision $\operatorname{sg}(\widehat{C})$ and predicted deformation magnitude $\operatorname{sg}(\|\mathbf{D}_t + \Delta\widehat{\mathbf{D}}\|)$ to evaluate slip likelihood under contact.

The training loss sums weighted cross-entropy for contact, Huber loss for deformation, and weighted cross-entropy for slip events. Stop-gradients ($\operatorname{sg}$) serve as the key structural element, preventing downstream losses from degrading upstream heads.

III-C Forecast-Guided Candidate Selection
Among valid sampled candidates, the system selects the best chunk $k^*$ that maximizes the video-based task progress score $\rho_{\mathrm{task}}^{(k)}$ while minimizing the sum of inconsistent contact cost $J_C^{(k)}$, excessive/unbalanced deformation cost $J_D^{(k)}$, and slip risk $J_R^{(k)}$.

III-D Online Forecast Verification
The selected forecast trajectory becomes an expected reference during execution. The system computes residuals against real observed tactile signals (contact error, slip error, and top-20 MAE of normal Z-axis deformation). It evaluates an anomaly score $S_{t+i}$ using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) fitted on nominal residuals. If this score exceeds a threshold for consecutive steps, execution aborts immediately, retracts to a safe pose, and triggers replanning.

captions.F3: Example progression of predicted tactile world states. In the top approach-to-contact transition phase, predicted contact aligns with actual contact timing, and slip risk exhibits a localized spike. In the bottom stable contact phase, the forecasts show high consistency with ground-truth RGB images and deformation.

sections.heading: From Fragile Chips to Rigid USBs: The Real-Robot Experimental Setup
sections.summary: This section outlines the experimental design to evaluate prediction accuracy, the benefit of the hierarchy, candidate selection gains, and online verification. Using an IMETA-Y1 robot with dual tactile sensors, over 360 real-robot trials were conducted across chip grasping, blackboard erasing, and USB insertion.
sections.details:
IV-A Robot Platform, Data, and Training
The experimental platform consists of an IMETA-Y1 robot arm equipped with two DM-Tac W2 tactile sensors on the gripper fingers and three RGB cameras across the workspace and wrist. The three evaluation tasks are:
- Chip grasping: Grasp and transfer a fragile potato chip to another plate without dropping or crushing it.
- Blackboard erasing: Press an eraser along a designated trajectory to clear over 80% of the target area.
- USB insertion: Fully insert a USB connector into a port without jamming until an LED illuminates.
For each task, 200 episodes (160 train, 20 val, 20 test) were collected and synchronized at 30 Hz. The tactile forecasting module was trained separately per task for 10,000 steps on 8 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

IV-B Metrics and Baselines
Tactile prediction quality was evaluated using contact F1 score, contact onset/offset frame errors, 3D deformation L2 error, Top-20 normal Z MAE, and slip AUPRC. Real-robot experiments compared the following methods:
- DreamZero: The original WAM without a tactile branch (single-candidate execution).
- Reactive Tactile: Reactive control using current tactile readings without future tactile forecasting.
- Task-Progress: Selecting among 4 candidates using only video-predicted task progress scores without tactile forecasts.
- Selection (Ours): Selecting among 4 candidates using HiTac-WAM hierarchical tactile forecasts and progress scores (without online verification).
- Full HiTac-WAM (Ours): The complete system combining candidate selection with runtime discrepancy monitoring and replanning.

Each task was tested over 30 trials (360 trials total) to strictly evaluate success rates.

captions.F4: Real-robot experimental platform setup. Two DM-Tac W2 tactile sensors are mounted opposing each other on the IMETA-Y1 gripper, accompanied by multiple cameras and task objects for chip grasping, blackboard erasing, and USB insertion.

sections.heading: Why Hierarchy Matters: Prediction Accuracy Gains and the 72.2% Success Rate
sections.summary: Results show that the physical hierarchy reduces 3D displacement error by 17.6% and improves slip AUPRC by 60.4%. On real-robot tasks, success rates jumped from 31.1% with single-candidate execution to 72.2% with the full system.
sections.details:
V-A Tactile Prediction Accuracy (Q1)
Across all tasks, HiTac-WAM achieved a mean contact F1 of 0.921, with onset and offset timing errors of about 2.1 to 2.3 frames (~60–87 ms). 3D deformation L2 error remained low at 0.058 mm. Slip AUPRC reached 0.247 on a highly imbalanced event occurring in only 1.39% of frames, far surpassing the chance level of 0.0139.

V-B Effects of Hierarchy and Conditioning (Q2)
Compared to single-head prediction or shared latent baselines, the directed hierarchy delivered clear performance gains:
- 3D deformation L2 error decreased by 17.6%, from 0.068 mm in the deformation-only predictor to 0.056 mm.
- Slip AUPRC improved by 60.4%, from 0.154 in the slip-only predictor to 0.247.
Intervention experiments shuffling or zeroing out the contact signal caused deformation error to degrade progressively (from 0.053 mm to 0.078 mm), proving the deformation head genuinely relies on contact cues. Meanwhile, adding the tactile heads had minimal impact on the base model, increasing video LPIPS by only 1.4% and action MAE by 0.9%.

V-C Forecast-Guided Candidate Selection (Q3)
On real robots, 'Selection' guided by HiTac-WAM forecasts attained a 61.1% success rate, doubling DreamZero's single-candidate rate of 31.1%. In a matched-budget comparison with 4 candidates, it also substantially outperformed selection by task progress alone (35.6%), confirming that tactile ranking is indispensable.

V-D Online Forecast Verification and Replanning (Q4)
The full HiTac-WAM system pushed success further from 61.1% to 72.2%. Out of 90 trials, discrepancy detection triggered replanning 18 times; 16 were genuine physical anomalies, and 12 of those recovered into successful task completions after safe retraction and retrying.

captions.F7: Online forecast verification log during real-robot execution. In the USB insertion task, the residual score $S_{t+i}$ between observations and predictions exceeds the threshold $\gamma_{\mathrm{task}}$ for three consecutive steps, triggering retraction, re-observation, and eventual successful insertion recovery.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook: Towards 'Imagine First, Verify Later' Tactile Control
sections.summary: HiTac-WAM integrates physically grounded hierarchical tactile forecasting with pre-execution candidate selection and runtime verification. Future extensions include validating forecasts on generated actions, uncertainty-aware slip modeling, and handling longer-horizon contact-rich tasks.
sections.details:
HiTac-WAM resolves the physical uncertainty at contact interfaces that previously hindered world action models by forecasting touch through a directed hierarchy: contact -> deformation -> slip. Experiments proved that explicitly enforcing physical dependencies greatly enhances prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the paradigm of 'imagining tactile outcomes beforehand to select the best action, then verifying them against reality to replan upon discrepancies' drastically boosts the robustness of contact-rich manipulation.

The authors note limitations: tactile forecast accuracy has not been evaluated independently on candidate actions sampled by the model itself outside of ground-truth datasets, and slip risk remains a relative ranking score rather than a calibrated probability for runtime alarming. Future work includes uncertainty-aware slip prediction and learning task-specific recovery policies instead of relying solely on heuristic retraction, paving the way for more sophisticated, long-horizon manipulation.

takeaways: When adding tactile forecasting to visual world models, organizing stages in a directed hierarchy (contact -> deformation -> slip) with stop-gradients significantly boosts accuracy.
A directed attention mask allows tactile queries to absorb video and action context without degrading the world model's visual and action generation capabilities.

Using tactile forecasts not only to rank candidate actions beforehand, but also as a time-synchronized reference to detect physical discrepancies and trigger replanning during execution, dramatically elevates real-robot success rates.
limitations: Tactile forecast quality on model-sampled, unexecuted action chunks has not been isolated and evaluated independently from ground-truth offline datasets.
Predicted slip risk functions as a relative score for candidate ranking rather than a calibrated probability suitable for definitive online alarms.
Anomaly recovery relies on a simple heuristic (retracting to a safe pose and replanning) rather than learning task-specific recovery policies.
